lead: A graph is connected when a path joins every pair of vertices. A spanning tree uses n−1 edges to connect all n vertices with no cycle. Parallel algorithms for connectivity and spanning trees use rounds: every vertex or every component makes a local choice at the same time, then the choices are merged. This appears in network planning, chip wiring and clustering. Only a few universities teach this at exam depth.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.5 for sorting an edge list, and Unit 1 for the PRAM and network models that run the rounds.

blocks.text: Take G = (V, E), with n = |V| vertices and m = |E| edges. Store E as an adjacency list, which lists each vertex's neighbours, or as an n × n adjacency matrix, which marks edge (u, v). A connected component is a maximal set of vertices joined by paths.

items: Give every vertex a parent pointer. Start with each vertex pointing to its lowest-numbered neighbour. Break a two-vertex cycle by keeping only the smaller vertex's choice, so every component has a root.
In one round, every vertex replaces its pointer by its parent's pointer. This is pointer jumping: a pointer that was k steps from the root becomes about k/2 steps away.
Repeat until every pointer points to the component root. Vertices with the same root are in one component.
For a BFS tree from a chosen root, expand one level at a time: all vertices on the current frontier read their unvisited neighbours in the same round.

blocks.text: rounds = O(log n); work per round = O(n + m) with an adjacency list, O(n²) with an adjacency matrix
blocks.where: n is the number of vertices, m is the number of edges. Total work is rounds × per-round work.

blocks.text: Let each edge carry a weight. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree of least total weight. Borůvka's algorithm works in rounds. A component is a set of vertices already joined by chosen edges.

items: For every component, find its minimum-weight outgoing edge: an edge with one end inside and one end outside.
All components choose at the same time. Add the distinct chosen edges. If several choices repeat an edge, add it once.
Hook the components joined by the new edges and contract each group into one supervertex. Edges inside a supervertex are discarded.
Stop when one component remains; then the chosen edges form an MST.

blocks.where: n is the number of vertices. Every round at least halves the number of components, because each component picks an edge to another component.

blocks.text: Prim and Kruskal add one edge at a time, so each step depends on the previous. Their parallel versions work on the edge list but still need a global order. A BFS tree is a spanning tree for an unweighted graph; with weights it need not be an MST.

figure.caption: Round 1 picks A–B 4, C–E 2 and C–D 7, giving groups {A,B} and {C,D,E}; round 2 adds A–C 8, so the MST weighs 4+2+7+8 = 21.

spec.aria: A five-vertex weighted graph for Borůvka's two rounds: round 1 picks A–B 4, C–E 2 and C–D 7, forming groups {A,B} and {C,D,E}; round 2 adds A–C 8, giving MST weight 21.

examples.question: Use Borůvka's algorithm on vertices A–E with edges A–B 4, A–C 8, B–C 11, C–D 7, C–E 2, D–E 9. Give each round's picks, the components after the round, the final MST and its total weight, and the number of rounds.
steps: Round 1: A picks A–B (4); B picks A–B (4); C picks C–E (2); D picks C–D (7); E picks C–E (2).
Distinct picks: A–B 4, C–E 2, C–D 7. Components: {A, B} and {C, D, E}.
Round 2: outgoing edges from {A,B} are A–C 8 and B–C 11, so it picks A–C 8. {C,D,E} also picks A–C 8. Add A–C once.
Now one component remains. Tree edges: A–B 4, C–E 2, C–D 7, A–C 8. Total = 4 + 2 + 7 + 8 = 21. Rounds = 2.
examples.answer: The MST is {A–B 4, C–E 2, C–D 7, A–C 8} with total weight 21, found in 2 rounds.

traps: In Borůvka, adding an edge whose two ends are already in one component makes a cycle; check the component labels before adding.
O(log n) rounds of O(n + m) work each is O((n + m) log n) total work, not O(log n).
Borůvka may add several edges in one round; Kruskal adds one edge at a time, so Kruskal is the sequential comparison.
A BFS tree is a spanning tree for an unweighted graph; it need not be a minimum spanning tree when edges have weights.
Pointer jumping needs a root or cycle break; two vertices pointing at each other forever is not a root.

quiz.q: Define connected component and spanning tree.
quiz.a: A connected component is a maximal set of vertices joined by paths. A spanning tree is a set of n−1 edges that connects all n vertices with no cycle.

quiz.q: Why does Borůvka's component count at least halve each round?
quiz.a: Every component picks one outgoing edge to another component, so components join in groups of at least two; hence the count is at most half.

quiz.q: In the example graph, list the distinct edges added in round 1 and the components after round 1.
Compare Borůvka with Kruskal for parallel execution.
quiz.a: Borůvka makes all component choices in parallel and adds many edges per round; Kruskal needs a global sorted order and adds one edge at a time, so its next step depends on the previous.

quiz.q: What does pointer jumping do to a parent pointer?
quiz.a: It replaces the pointer by its parent's pointer, halving the remaining distance to the root in one round.

quiz.q: For n = 1024 vertices, what is the maximum number of Borůvka rounds by the halving bound?
Why is connectivity work O(n²) per round with an adjacency matrix but O(n+m) with an adjacency list?
quiz.a: A matrix round scans n² cells; an adjacency list round reads each vertex and each edge once, total n+m.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parallel connectivity and MST are building blocks in graph processing systems for social networks, road maps and network design. GPU and multi-core libraries run Borůvka-style rounds on edge lists. Distributed graph frameworks split vertices across machines and use message passing for the same choices. Search for parallel connected components, Borůvka GPU, and distributed minimum spanning tree.
